new_statements.quote: 14° Accentuation. — L'accent tonique n'existe pas à proprement parler en vaï; on doit seulement faire attention de ne jamais accentuer les particules. Mais il y a des longues et des brèves qui se font largement sentir, et de plus une intonation spéciale et assez curieuse, qu'il est impossible de définir exactement, et qui consiste le plus généralement à prononcer la dernière syllabe de chaque proposition sur un ton plus aigu que les autres, et la syllabe finale de la phrase au contraire sur un ton plus bas que le ton général. Cette sorte de chant est sensible surtout dans la conversation des femmes.
new_statements.translation: 14. Accentuation. — Strictly speaking, tonic (word) stress does not exist in Vai; one need only take care never to stress the particles. But there are long and short [syllables/vowels] that are strongly felt, and in addition a special and rather curious intonation, impossible to define exactly, which consists most generally in pronouncing the last syllable of each clause on a higher pitch than the others, and the final syllable of the sentence, on the contrary, on a lower pitch than the general pitch. This sort of chant is especially noticeable in the conversation of women.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Vai (catalog-all-2026-09-12) has an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so this is the first sourced stress statement for the language: the source denies word stress and describes only clause/sentence-final pitch movement plus vowel length. Note that Delafosse (1899) is a pre-tonological description; he does not identify lexical tone, so his 'no accent' statement should be read as 'no stress accent noticed', not as a modern claim that Vai lacks tone.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Delafosse states that Vai has no word-level tonic accent properly speaking; the only rule he gives is negative (particles are never stressed). What he does hear is vowel/syllable length (long vs. short) and a phrase-level intonation contour: the last syllable of each clause is raised in pitch and the final syllable of the whole sentence is lowered below the general pitch. He does not recognise lexical tone; the pitch phenomena he describes are clause/sentence-final, not word-level.
new_statements.exceptions: none beyond the instruction never to stress particles; the pitch pattern is said to be 'impossible to define exactly' and most audible in women's speech
new_statements.identity_note: Delafosse describes the Vai of the Cape Mount region between the Half-Cape-Mount river (Liberia) and the Sulima river (Sierra Leone), plus settlements near Monrovia (offprint p. 3, p. 4); no dialect split is named. Language of publication French; author's own Latin-based transcription with no tone or stress marks.

tone_statements.quote: Similar but not identical THM involving W2 lowering is even found in the Vai-Kono sub-taxa of Central Mande. In Vai, W2 is also lowered to {L}, which remains [L] after another L (12a,b). However, when W1’s lexical melody ends in a H, H appears on the first TBU of W2, although only after a lexically /LH/ W1 (12c,d), but not after a lexically /H/ W1 (12e,f).

audit.reasoning: The classification 'tonal' (two discrete level tones, all four disyllabic sequences contrastive, grammatical tone, no stress/accent mentioned) rests on Welmers 1976, the standard and only modern reference grammar of Vai, with dedicated Tones and Intonations chapters; all three Welmers quotations and the Koelle 1854 historical 'accent' quotations were confirmed verbatim at the stated pages in the copies we hold. Glottolog's 68-item bibliography and CrossRef contain no later phonology, prosody or instrumental study of Vai; the only later linguistic work found (Tröbs 2014, Kastenholz 2019 dictionary) follows Welmers' tonal analysis and is silent on stress. Nothing suggests a reclassify. sources.note: Notes that the dictionary gives no description of the basic phonology ('tonal oppositions, the presence or absence of tonal processes'), points to tone alternations visible in examples (kɔ̀ŋ 'tree' vs kɔ́m ɓìlà) left unexplained, and to entries printed without tonal notation (Ɓowakai, ɓunɗu) with no statement whether the missing tone is phonological or a gap in Klingenheben's data. Useful as evidence that the 2019 dictionary is tone-marked but contains no tonology.

sources.quote: The description of Vai tonology in Welmers (1976) is fairly extensive and deals with the subject of compounds in detail. The tonal system of Vai is such that the language has both H and L tones and four major tonal melodies: H, L, LH, and HL. Certain more complex combinations of tones are possible in morphologically‑complex words.
sources.note: Summarises Vai tonology after Welmers 1976 - H and L tones, four major word melodies H, L, LH, HL, more complex combinations in morphologically complex words; compound (replacive) tone: W1 keeps its melody and W2 is neutralised to [L], except that after a lexically /LH/ W1 the W1 surfaces [L] and W2 becomes [HL] (H spread), so Vai is a hybrid of the author's Type 1 and Type 2 replacive-tone patterns; eight Vai compound examples in (18).
